## Chapter Summary

SQL lets an auditor test entire populations across the tables of a process, and a population test finds the actual exceptions rather than an error rate. Its power depends on its inputs, so every test begins by reconciling the population to the ledger. The source-document columns of the ledger allow a trace in two directions. An anti-join from the ledger to a document table finds postings with no document, which tests existence, and an anti-join from the documents to the ledger finds documents never posted, which tests completeness. UNION ALL combines the results of several tests into one labeled list of exceptions. Comparing a document's date with the posting date of its ledger rows tests cutoff.

A three-way match compares the quantities ordered, received, and invoiced at the level of the purchase order line, after the receipts and invoices of each line are summed, and it compares invoice prices with order prices within a tolerance chosen in advance. Goods received but not yet invoiced are an accrual, and their value should agree with the ledger. Approval tests join each document to its approver and compare it with the approver's limit, employment dates, and role, and with the document's creator. They also reveal how concentrated the approval of a process is. Tests of the records behind a cost follow the chain from the time clock through the labor record and the payroll register to the payment and the ledger. They distinguish isolated exceptions, which are failures in the operation of a control, from systematic patterns, which point to its design. Chapter 8's duplicate, sequence, and first-digit tests translate into self-joins, LAG, and aggregates, and a documented library of such tests can be rerun every period.

Applied to the audit committee's question, the tests found that the ledger's populations reconcile and nearly every posting traces to a document and back. The six postings that do not trace record cash paid without a payment record, two of those payments for an employee who had left. The purchasing chain matches, and its unbilled receipts agree with the ledger, but its approvals show exceptions and a single point of failure. The manufacturing hours behind the variance were clocked, approved above the overtime threshold, and paid, and the manufacturing payroll ties to the ledger, so the variance is a real cost. The audit also found that a growing share of direct labor is recorded against operations that had already ended, mostly at Packing, so the operation-level records cannot show where the extra hours were spent.
